The pulmo- nary hypertension and altered vasoreactivity lead to a right-to-left shunting of blood across the patent ductus ar- teriosus or foramen ovale and this often results in critical hypoxaemia. Management generally involves high-frequency oscillat- ory ventilation (to achieve optimal lung inflation) and, if necessary, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Treat- ment to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance may also be tried. Mechanical hyperventilation has been used to induce alkalosis, since this reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction; intravenous sodium bicarbonate may be an alternative.40 Inhaled nitric oxide which is a potent, selective pulmonary vasodilator, is also widely used.41 Studies42-46 have shown that it can cause marked improvement in oxygenation and a reduction in the need for extracorporeal membrane oxy- genation, but no effect on mortality has been found. Al- though there have been concerns that use of inhaled nitric oxide might adversely affect neurodevelopmental out- come more than conventional therapy, this has not been confirmed in infants followed up for up to 2 years.47,48 Use of inhaled nitric oxide in combination with high-frequency oscillatory ventilation may have additional benefits.49 Nitric oxide is not effective in all patients and alternatives may be required.50,51 Intravenous vasodilators have been used, although, as discussed above, this is generally limit- ed by their systemic effects. Tolazoline has been most commonly used, and may be given intravenously or by the endotracheal route. Intravenous epoprostenol is also used; it has also been given by inhalation,52,53 which may reduce systemic effects. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors may have a role; dipyridamole has been used, and there have been reports54,55 of benefit with sildenafil. Other vasodilators that have been tried include intravenous adenosine,56,57 in- travenous magnesium sulfate,58-60 and inhaled sodium ni- troprusside,61 but none of these has an established role. 1.
